question: What minerals besides calcium help restless legs?
answer_short: Wallach treats restless leg like osteoporosis — adding magnesium, boron, copper, sulfur, selenium and strontium, and cutting excess phosphate, fat and salt.
answer_full:
Besides calcium, Wallach reaches for magnesium, boron, copper, sulfur, selenium, and strontium. He treats restless leg the same way he treats osteoporosis, which in his framework is fundamentally a calcium-deficiency disease: when the diet runs chronically short of calcium, the body pulls it back out of the bones to keep blood levels steady, thinning the skeleton. But calcium can't do the job alone — Wallach says holding and building bone depends on those co-factor minerals alongside it, which is why his formula corrects all of them together rather than just handing you calcium.

The other half of his approach is cutting what works against those minerals: excess phosphorus (which he says raises the body's calcium requirement), fluoride, cadmium, dietary fats, and salt. And the pattern isn't unique to restless leg — Wallach applies the very same six-mineral cluster, plus the same cut in excess phosphorus and dietary fat, to sciatica, another lower-body complaint he files under calcium-deficiency low-back problems.

question: Can moldy grain or a fungal toxin cause tinnitus?
answer_short: Yes—Wallach notes that ergot (a fungus on rye) produces tinnitus among its symptoms by constricting blood vessels, cutting circulation to poorly-supplied tissues like the ears.
answer_full:
Yes. Wallach ties tinnitus to ergot poisoning — ergot being a fungus whose alkaloids, ergotamine and ergocristine, work by clamping down on blood vessels, contracting the smooth muscle in their walls. That vasoconstriction is the engine of the whole poisoning: as blood flow is choked off, ringing in the ears shows up as just one symptom in a wide cluster that also includes vertigo, headaches, hallucinations, mania, psychosis, vomiting, and the eerie feeling of ants crawling under the skin (formication). At its extreme the same squeezing can cut circulation off completely and cause dry gangrene — tissue that dies for lack of blood.

Two details make the picture click. The ergot alkaloid ergotamine is related to LSD, which is why Wallach's symptom list runs to hallucinations and psychosis and not just physical damage. And that vessel-contracting action isn't only a poison: ergotamine doubles as a migraine drug, easing the headache through the very same tightening of the blood vessels.

Ergot is only one of several roots Wallach traces for ringing ears — others, in his telling, run from high blood pressure to bone loss in the skull to drug side effects.
claim_text: Wallach documents that ergot-fungus alkaloids cause tinnitus (alongside vertigo, headaches, and hallucinations) through vasoconstriction that starves poorly-vascularized tissues such as the ears.

question: Is boron important for a man's testosterone and sexual health?
answer_short: Yes — Wallach says boron is essential for the proper functioning of the testes, ovaries, and adrenal glands, the organs that produce your sex hormones.
answer_full:
Yes. Wallach counts boron among the trace minerals the body must have, and its job runs right through a man's sexual machinery: it's essential for the proper functioning of the testes and adrenal glands — the organs that manufacture the sex hormones — and, in his framework, for keeping the blood levels of testosterone and estrogen where they should be. So a shortfall doesn't just weaken bone; it can undercut the very system that makes testosterone.

Boron is an easy nutrient to miss. Wallach describes it as a scarce, non-metallic trace mineral that never turns up pure in nature — you only find it locked into compounds like borax and boric acid — and it wasn't accepted as essential for humans until 1990. Beyond the hormone role, he ties it to bone metabolism and the efficient use of calcium and magnesium.

Wallach also names a second lever for the same problem: cholesterol. Because the body builds testosterone out of cholesterol, he warns that pushing cholesterol too low backfires on men — a deficiency, in his words, "will turn hubby into a TV watching steer who is totally disinterested in sex."
claim_text: Boron is essential for the proper functioning of the testes, ovaries, and adrenal glands — the very organs that make a man's sex hormones.

and magnesium and for the proper functioning of the ovaries, testes, and adrenal.
glands.

question: What did women use for menopause before modern medicine?
answer_short: Wallach tells how Lydia Pinkham's herbal compound, built on an old Native American recipe, was sold for menopausal symptoms, PMS and other women's complaints — and worked well enough to make her famous, an example of the herbal remedies orthodox medicine brushed aside.
answer_full:
Before modern medicine, Wallach says, one of the most popular answers to menopausal symptoms was a bottled herbal remedy: Lydia Pinkham's "Vegetable and Herbal Extract for Women's Complaints." Pinkham was a Quaker missionary who built her patent medicine on an ancient Native American herbal recipe and sold it through newspaper and magazine ads, marketing it across the whole range of women's complaints — PMS, dysmenorrhea (painful periods), amenorrhea (missed periods), menopausal symptoms and infertility. Wallach recounts that it worked so well the Harvard Glee Club sang songs about her abilities, and she became an American icon.

For Wallach it's an example of the effective herbal remedies orthodox medicine brushed aside. In his telling it belongs to a much older tradition — herbal medicine, the ancient system of using plants to prevent and cure disease that runs through American Indian medicine, Traditional Chinese medicine and American folk medicine alike. And the orthodox alternative was far harsher: for the cyclical emotional symptoms of women, he notes, the historical treatment was the hysterectomy — removing the ovaries and uterus, which "cured" the symptoms but forced an abrupt menopause. Against a bottle of herbal extract sold cheaply in the newspaper, it's easy to see why women flocked to Pinkham.

question: Can a thyroid or iodine deficiency be linked to varicose veins?
answer_short: In his African clinic Wallach saw iodine and copper deficiency together produce varicose veins, aneurysms, anemia, miscarriages, and goiter in adults.
answer_full:
Yes. In his clinic work in Africa, Wallach saw iodine and copper deficiency together produce a whole cluster of adult problems — and varicose veins were one of them, alongside anemia, aneurysms, miscarriages, and goiter (the swollen thyroid that is the classic sign of iodine shortage).

The vein damage itself traces mostly to copper. Copper is the cofactor for lysyl oxidase — the enzyme that gives blood vessels their tensile strength and builds the strong, elastic fibers in artery walls. Starve the body of copper and those walls weaken, stretch, and bulge: they show up as varicose veins, spider veins, hemorrhoids (which Wallach counts as simply the rectal-and-anal form of a varicose vein) and, at worst, aneurysms — rupture-prone weak spots in the vessel wall. His favorite illustration is a flock of turkeys that were dying of ruptured aortic aneurysms; the deaths stopped once copper was doubled in their feed.

Because the same shortage shows up in pigment as well as connective tissue, Wallach points to premature gray, white, or silver hair as the first visible sign of copper deficiency — a clue often worth noticing before the veins are.

osteomalacia in children and arthritis, and osteoporosis and kidney stones in
adults. lodine and copper deficiency produced anemia, varicose veins, aneurysms,
miscarriages, and goiter in adults.

question: Can gluten or a damaged gut cause skin problems like rosacea?
answer_short: Wallach says gluten damages the gut lining, and the resulting malabsorption drives skin diseases like rosacea, dermatitis, eczema, and psoriasis — it is what you absorb, not just what you eat.
answer_full:
Yes — this is central to how Wallach explains skin disease. He argues gluten isn't really an allergy but a "contact enteritis": the proteins in small grains irritate the gut lining the same way poison ivy irritates skin — no one is truly allergic to poison ivy, yet almost everyone reacts to it. That constant irritation gradually destroys the intestinal villi, the gut-lining structures that absorb your nutrients, until as much as 85-90% of the absorptive surface can be gone. At that point the body starves for nutrients even on a good diet, and the skin — which depends on those nutrients — breaks out. Wallach ties rosacea, dermatitis, eczema, psoriasis, and acne all to this malabsorption, which is exactly why he says "you are what you absorb," not just what you eat.

He points to the essential fatty acids as one concrete link: when the damaged gut can't absorb them, that deficiency by itself produces dry, cracked skin, dermatitis, eczema, psoriasis, rosacea, and acne. So his approach works both ends — remove the irritant with a gluten-free (and often cow's-milk-free) diet, and rebuild what's missing. For eczema specifically he adds zinc at 50 mg three times a day and folic acid at 3-5 mg a day.

question: Does cobalt play a role in the thyroid?
answer_short: Yes -- Wallach says cobalt is a necessary cofactor for making thyroid hormone, so it is another mineral the thyroid depends on besides iodine.
answer_full:
Yes. Wallach says cobalt is a necessary cofactor for producing thyroid hormone — one more mineral the thyroid leans on besides iodine. The reason traces back to what cobalt actually is inside the body: a single cobalt atom sits at the very center of vitamin B12, so your requirement for cobalt is really a requirement for the finished B12 molecule. That cobalt/B12 pairing does some of the body's most fundamental work — building DNA and RNA, forming red blood cells, and making the myelin that insulates nerves — and, among those jobs, helping the body manufacture the thyroid hormone thyroxine.

This fits Wallach's larger point about the thyroid: he insists it needs far more than iodine. He says the gland requires all 90 essential nutrients to make thyroxin properly. Iodine combines with the amino acid tyrosine to form the hormone, copper is a required cofactor for actually using that iodine, and molybdenum and cobalt round out the supporting cast. For cobalt itself he prefers 250 to 400 micrograms a day, well above the conventional 3-to-4 microgram allowance.
claim_text: Wallach says cobalt is a necessary cofactor the body needs to produce thyroid hormone.
verbatim:
Cobalt is also a necessary cofactor for the production of thyroid
hormone.

question: What diet does Wallach recommend to prevent dementia?
answer_short: Wallach's anti-dementia diet cuts fried foods, processed meats and added oils and has you eat 4-6 eggs per 100 pounds of body weight a day.
answer_full:
Wallach's anti-dementia diet is really two moves: take out the foods he blames for damaging the brain, and add eggs as raw building material. Because he frames dementia not as one disease but as at least four distinct nutritional diseases — vascular dementia, Korsakoff's syndrome, Wernicke-Korsakoff's, and Alzheimer's — the same dietary changes run across all of them.

What comes out: no fried foods, no processed meats, and no added oils. In his telling these are the everyday foods that do the harm — fried and overcooked ("burnt") foods and oxidized oils drive free-radical damage and load the body with trans fatty acids, heterocyclic amines, and acrylamides, while nitrate-preserved processed meats add their own toxins and inflame the lining of the brain's arteries.

What goes in: 4-6 eggs per hundred pounds of body weight a day — poached, soft-boiled, or scrambled in butter — to give the brain the raw material it needs, alongside all 90 essential nutrients, antioxidants beyond 100,000 ORAC points a day, and the omega-3 fats DHA and EPA to support the neurotransmitters of memory and cognition. Wallach points to a Johns Hopkins randomized, double-blind ten-year study (published 2004, on nearly 5,000 people over 65) that he says showed a special diet plus nutrient supplementation cut Alzheimer's risk by 78%.
claim_text: As part of his anti-dementia approach to Alzheimer's, Wallach's diet cuts out fried foods, processed meats and added oils and has you eat 4 to 6 eggs per hundred pounds of body weight a day.

question: Can a copper deficiency make hair dry and brittle?
answer_short: Yes — Wallach lists dry, brittle hair (the 'steely wool' seen in copper-deficient sheep), along with white, gray and silver hair, among the signs of copper deficiency.
answer_full:
Yes — dry, brittle hair sits on Wallach's list of copper-deficiency signs, and the comparison he reaches for is an animal one: he calls it the human version of the "steely wool" seen in copper-deficient sheep, hair gone coarse and lifeless for want of the mineral.

The same shortage usually shows in the hair's color, too. Wallach calls premature white, gray, or silver hair the first visible sign of low copper, and the reason is that copper is the cofactor pigment-making depends on: the enzyme tyrosinase works on the amino acid tyrosine to build melanin — the pigment that colors hair and skin — and that reaction can't proceed without copper. Run low, and the pigment fails, so the hair turns white, silver, or gray. (Red hair is his exception — its color comes from an iron-based pigment rather than ordinary melanin.) Copper does structural work as well, driving the enzyme lysyl oxidase that gives connective tissue its tensile strength, which is why Wallach ties the same deficiency to sagging skin, varicose veins, and aneurysms.

question: Can poor nutrient absorption cause constipation?
answer_short: Wallach lists constipation among the diseases caused by malabsorption, summed up in his rule 'you are what you absorb.'
answer_full:
Yes — Wallach lists constipation among a long roster of diseases that all trace back to one root: malabsorption, the failure to actually take up nutrients from your food even when the diet itself is adequate. He sums the whole idea up in his rule, "you are what you absorb."

The mechanism he points to is damage to the gut lining. Wallach frames gluten intolerance as a "contact enteritis" — an irritant reaction of grain proteins against the intestinal wall, the way poison ivy irritates skin — that gradually strips away the villi, the tiny finger-like folds that do the absorbing. Celiac-type damage, he says, can destroy up to 85–90% of that absorptive surface, so the body starves for nutrients on an otherwise reasonable diet, and constipation is one of the downstream results. It can also arrive by more than one route in his framework: he counts hypothyroidism among malabsorption's diseases too, and constipation is one of the classic signs of an underactive thyroid.

question: Can moldy grain (ergot) cause vertigo?
answer_short: Yes - Wallach describes ergot poisoning (from fungus-infected grain, the toxin behind 'St. Anthony's fire') as causing vertigo and tinnitus along with seizures, hallucinations, and gangrene.
answer_full:
Yes — Wallach lists vertigo and tinnitus (ringing in the ears) among the symptoms of ergot poisoning, the toxin that grows on fungus-infected grain. The fungus produces a family of compounds he calls the ergotamine-ergocristine alkaloids, and their central action is vasoconstriction — clamping down on blood vessels. That squeeze on the circulation is what drives the poisoning's most dramatic end point, dry gangrene, where tissue dies once its blood supply is choked off.

Around the vertigo and tinnitus, Wallach paints a whole-body picture: painful seizures and spasms, headaches, vomiting and diarrhea, hallucinations, mania and psychosis, and unsettling skin sensations — paresthesia (itching and prickling) and formication (the feeling of ants crawling under the skin).

The same alkaloid, he notes, isn't only a poison. Ergotamine is a drug used to treat migraine headaches — an ergot-fungus alkaloid related to LSD — and it works by the very mechanism that makes it dangerous: contracting the smooth muscle of the blood vessels.

question: Could a thyroid problem be behind my heavy periods?
answer_short: Heavy or more frequent periods can be a thyroid clue: Wallach lists them among the symptoms of hypothyroidism (Hashimoto's), alongside fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, hair loss and depression.
answer_full:
Yes — Wallach lists heavier or more frequent periods among the symptoms of an underactive thyroid (hypothyroidism, or Hashimoto's disease), right alongside fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, hair loss and depression. The link runs through the thyroid hormone itself: Wallach describes thyroxin — built from iodine plus the amino acid tyrosine — as the regulator of a whole spread of systems, the reproductive system among them, along with general metabolism, heart rate and body temperature. So when the gland slows down, the menstrual cycle is one of the things that drifts.

The mirror image makes the pattern clearer: in Wallach's telling an over-active thyroid (hyperthyroidism, Graves' disease) does the opposite, producing lighter or less frequent periods. He traces the underlying driver largely to too little iodine — he argues intake is usually low to begin with, and that salt-restriction on medical advice has made hypothyroidism epidemic — with copper needed as a cofactor to actually use the iodine, and goitrogen foods like cruciferous vegetables and gluten interfering with the gland.

question: Is gum disease caused by bacteria, or by a nutritional deficiency?
answer_short: Wallach puts gingivitis in the same category as scurvy, beriberi and pellagra — diseases the medical world first blamed on an infectious germ but that turned out to be caused by a nutritional deficiency.
answer_full:
Wallach's answer is nutritional deficiency, not the germs. He files gum disease alongside scurvy, beriberi and pellagra — a whole class of diseases medicine first pinned on an infectious agent before they turned out to be deficiencies (he adds cardiomyopathy, Bell's palsy and multiple sclerosis to the same list).

What's actually failing, in his telling, isn't gum tissue being invaded — it's bone loss underneath the gums. As that bone recedes, the gum has nothing to anchor it and pulls back. He rejects the standard dental explanation that food particles packing between the teeth and gums are to blame, and offers the animal kingdom as proof: cows, horses, dogs and cats never floss, brush, or use fluoride mouthwash, yet the veterinary profession eliminated periodontal disease in them purely through nutrition. Pellagra is his historical template — once feared as a contagious, insect-borne illness (like malaria or yellow fever), it turned out to be a simple shortage of niacin, vitamin B3, that cleared when eggs and milk were added back to sufferers' diets.

So his treatment is dietary, not antiseptic: correct the calcium-to-phosphorus ratio by dropping phosphate-laden soft drinks, then supplement calcium at 2,000 mg and magnesium at 1,000 mg a day.

question: Can low vitamin D cause gum disease and tooth loss?
answer_short: Wallach lists periodontal disease right next to osteoporosis, bone spurs and arthritis as a problem of vitamin D deficiency, fitting his view that gum disease is really bone loss in the jaw.
answer_full:
Yes — Wallach lists periodontal disease as one of the health problems of vitamin D deficiency, grouping it with osteoporosis, bone spurs and arthritis. Those belong together because of his core view of gum disease: it isn't really a gum problem at all but bone loss in the jaw. The alveolar bone — the bone that anchors each tooth root — dissolves out from under the gums, so the gums recede and the teeth loosen. He calls it, in effect, osteoporosis of the jaw.

Vitamin D is the link. Its job is to absorb, metabolize and properly deposit calcium and phosphorus into the bones and teeth, so when it runs low that jawbone can't be maintained and begins to give way. Wallach calls today's near-universal vitamin D shortage a "physician-caused disease" — the combined result of being told to avoid the sun, wear sunblock and covering clothing, cut dietary cholesterol like egg yolks and dairy, and skip mineral supplements.
claim_text: Wallach lists periodontal disease alongside osteoporosis, bone spurs and arthritis as a health problem of vitamin D deficiency.

question: Can a stomach ulcer kill you?
answer_short: It can. Wallach recounts that Linus Pauling's father, Herman Pauling, died suddenly of a perforated gastric ulcer complicated by peritonitis - the ulcer ate through the stomach wall, spilling its contents into the abdomen. It's a reminder that an ignored ulcer can turn deadly fast.
answer_full:
Yes — Wallach drives the point home with a famous death. Linus Pauling's father, Herman Pauling, died suddenly of a perforated gastric ulcer complicated by peritonitis: the sore burrowed clean through the stomach wall — which is what "perforated" means — and the inflammation that followed is what actually killed him.

An ulcer turns deadly in two ways: it can perforate like Pauling's, or it can bleed. Wallach's home warning sign for the second is unmistakable — a "coffee-ground" stool or vomit means the ulcer is already bleeding, and he says to get to a hospital immediately before the patient bleeds to death.

The hopeful flip side is that Wallach doesn't blame stress or the mythical "vitamin U" for ulcers in the first place. He points to infection with Helicobacter pylori — the same bacterium veterinarians found causing gastric ulcers in pigs — as the real cause, and says a course of antibiotics for four to six weeks is the preferred treatment over surgery. Caught in time, the thing that killed Herman Pauling is curable.
claim_text: Wallach recounts that Linus Pauling's father, Herman Pauling, died suddenly of a perforated gastric ulcer complicated by peritonitis - a reminder that an untreated ulcer can burrow all the way through the stomach wall and kill quickly.

question: Can contaminated grain make your skin tingle and crawl?
answer_short: Wallach recounts ergot poisoning from moldy rye -- the likely cause of the Salem 'bewitchments' -- producing paresthesia (itching and prickling), formication (a feeling of ants crawling under the skin), and even dry gangrene of the fingers and toes.
answer_full:
Yes. Wallach describes exactly that from ergot poisoning, the toxin a grain fungus produces. Two of its signature signs are paresthesia — itching and prickling — and formication, the unnerving feeling that ants are crawling under the skin. Those sit inside a much larger symptom storm he lists: painful seizures and spasms, diarrhea, vomiting, headaches, vertigo, tinnitus (ringing in the ears), and mind-level effects like mania, psychosis, and hallucinations.

The gravest damage, though, is circulatory rather than sensory. The fungus's alkaloids — ergotamine and ergocristine — drive vasoconstriction, a hard clamping-down of the blood vessels. Starve the fingers and toes of blood long enough and the tissue dies, producing dry gangrene in the extremities.

That crawling-skin feeling isn't unique to poisoning, either. Wallach ties the same paresthesia, especially in the hands and feet, to a biotin deficiency — showing up there alongside hair loss, skin lesions around the nose and mouth, and depression.

question: Can poor nutrient absorption cause rosacea?
answer_short: Wallach places rosacea among the many conditions that arise from poor nutrient absorption, captured in his phrase 'you are what you absorb' -- pointing to what the gut takes in rather than the skin itself.
answer_full:
In Wallach's framework, yes -- but he'd say the trouble isn't really in your skin. He files rosacea among a long list of conditions that stem from poor nutrient absorption, summed up in his phrase "you are not what you eat -- you are what you absorb." The redness, in other words, is a downstream sign of a gut that isn't taking nutrients in, not a disease of the face itself.

How does absorption fail? Wallach ties it to food allergies that cause celiac-type damage to the gut wall, which then blocks the essential nutrients the body needs from getting through. He spells out this gut-skin link most fully for the skin conditions sitting right beside rosacea in that same list -- dermatitis and eczema -- where he says the great majority of patients have wheat-gluten and cow's-milk allergies that raise the same lesions in the small-intestine lining, producing serious malabsorption. His fix in those cases treats the gut rather than the skin: a gluten-free, cow's-milk-free diet plus betaine hydrochloride (a supplemental form of stomach acid) and digestive enzymes to restore absorption.

That same list also places rosacea alongside psoriasis, asthma, diabetes and osteoporosis, among dozens of others -- a measure of how broadly Wallach applies the idea that health is set by what the gut absorbs, not simply what you eat.
